input: Liquid-liquid extraction is a well-established separation technique that can be used to recover acetic acid from an aqueous stream by transferring it into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient of acetic acid between the two phases, defined as its concentration in the organic phase divided by its concentration in the aqueous phase, is 0.92 at a temperature of 25 °C. A coefficient below unity indicates that the acid preferentially remains in the aqueous phase at equilibrium in a single contact, meaning that the recovery achieved by the design is built up through staging rather than through the coefficient alone. In a countercurrent cascade, the aqueous stream and the solvent flow in opposite directions through the stages, so that the freshest solvent comes into contact with the most depleted aqueous stream, while the loaded solvent leaves in contact with the incoming feed, ensuring that each stage operates against the most favourable composition difference that the arrangement can offer. The design employs a total of 7 countercurrent stages. On this basis, the predicted recovery is 94% of the acetic acid present in the feed. It is important to note that this prediction rests on two key assumptions, namely that every stage reaches equilibrium and that the mutual solubility of the two phases is negligible. Neither of these assumptions has been verified using the actual solvents. Consequently, the predicted recovery of 94% should be regarded as a design figure with its conditions attached: it holds where the stages equilibrate and the phases remain effectively immiscible, and the recovery that would be obtained with the actual solvents will differ wherever either assumption fails to hold, by an amount that the stated data do not determine.
